title: Common Core R.CCR.5 Explained
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart unpacks anchor standard R.CCR.5, analyzing text structure, by showing the kinds of questions that get students thinking about how parts relate to the whole. For novels, he walks through an awkward early scene in All Quiet on the Western Front and uses paired questions and a second close reading to lead students to its link to the book's theme and suspense. For columns he proposes questions about thesis, naysayers, and beginnings and endings, using a Leonard Pitts piece. For poems and primary sources he offers further question sets, noting that the goal of poetry is to see the impact of structure rather than to produce English majors. He concludes that the standard is taught through complex texts, redundant literacy instruction, and well-designed questions.
points: A single jarring scene, read closely twice and framed by a pointed question, can lead students to discover a novel's theme and structure on their own.
Columns teach structure because their arguments do not follow the five-paragraph template students are drilled on.
Poetry is useful for showing structure's effect on meaning, not for producing future English majors.
In history classes, structure helps students identify what kind of document a primary source is.
quotes: In one of the novel’s early scenes, we find protagonist Paul sitting in a meadow with a couple of his comrades-in-arms. Everything is pleasant about the scene — they are sitting in a circle, playing cards, laughing, talking — except for one jarring detail: they are sitting on boxes with holes in the tops with their pants around their ankles.

I will remind students that, in order to understand how this scene relates to the novel as a whole, we’ll have to look not just at what the scene says, but also what it hints at and what it doesn’t explicitly say. In teacherspeak, we’ll need to infer.

Through asking the right questions, students are led to discover that this scene is not flippant, but rather that it hints at the theme of the book: World War I was unlike anything humanity had ever seen; it devastated the men in death and life. Furthermore, this scene builds suspense at the start of the novel.

My primary goal in teaching poetry is not to mold my students into future English majors, but rather to equip them with the ability to see the impact that structure has on a text. Poems can help with that.
Is this an advertisement? A comic? A political cartoon? An argument? A legal document? Ask students to figure these things out for themselves, in part by using the structure of the document itself.
